1.pericope_label: Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God: be not rash with thy mouth

schools.summary: Henry reads the verse as autobiography, the writer sending us to the temple he had himself built at vast expense, the one work he did not repent of and yet does not mention lest he seem to reflect on it with pride, and adds that disappointment in the creature should turn us to the Creator, since in the word and in prayer there is a balm for every wound.

Gill takes the singular foot as put for the plural, rules out both keeping the foot from going in and a slow approach since the motion should be quick and zealous, and refers the phrase to the pulling off of the shoes commanded on holy ground, while keeping the dream and the many words to a plain comparison.

Clarke notes that the Hebrew and all the versions join the first verse to the preceding chapter, translates the difficult clause literally so that none of them have knowledge about doing evil and explains it from an old paraphrase about men who offer gifts for their sins without turning from their works, and sets a passage of devotional verse beside the warning against rashness; Wesley makes the feet the thoughts and affections, keeps the received sense of the difficult clause, and argues from the seventh verse that the multitude of words means vowing rather than prayer.

Ellicott records the Hebrew verse division and argues that a new section nevertheless begins here from the sudden use of the second person singular, and holds that the received English of the last clause is one of the expedients resorted to in order to get a better meaning, the most natural translation being that they know not how to do evil; Keil and Delitzsch deny that priests are in view at the word for being taught, hold that the priesthood did not belong to the teaching class in the sense of preaching, and date the entry of preaching into worship to the synagogue after the exile.

debates: Where does the chapter begin? Clarke reports that the Hebrew and all the versions attach the first verse to the preceding chapter; Ellicott records the same division and argues that a new section nevertheless begins here, since the proverbs that follow are in the second person singular, a form not used before in the book, and finds no obvious connection with what precedes.

What does the last clause of the first verse mean? Ellicott holds that the most natural translation is that they know not how to do evil, that is are incapable of it, which would make the subject those ready to hear rather than the fools, and calls the received English one of the expedients resorted to in order to get a better meaning, reporting a third rendering besides; Clarke translates literally in the same direction and explains it from an old paraphrase about men who offer gifts for their sins without turning from their works; Wesley keeps the received sense and makes the fools insensible of the sinfulness of their thoughts.

Is the multitude of words prayer or vowing? Wesley argues that it is vowing, since the following verses are about vows and the seventh verse reads as a comment on the third, which makes it probable that both are to be understood of vows rather than prayers; Gill and Clarke keep the comparison general, that as the day’s business breeds confused dreams so many words betray a foolish heart.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch use the word for being taught to deny that the priesthood belonged to the teaching class in the sense of preaching, holding that priestly instruction limited itself to the performance of the law already given and to questions of legal practice, that preaching was never part of the temple worship at all, and that it entered worship for the first time after the exile in the synagogue, the preachers of the older covenant having been the prophets.
Keil and Delitzsch report that the rabbis declined to treat this book as apocryphal because it begins and ends with words of the law.

Henry treats the verse as autobiography, the writer sending readers to the temple he had built at vast expense, the only one of his works he did not repent of, and not naming it lest he seem to reflect on it with pride.

Gill rules out two senses of keeping the foot before offering his own, denying both that it means keeping the foot from going in and that it means a slow approach, since the motion should be quick and zealous.
themes: a chapter that begins in the previous one
a received rendering called an expedient
preaching dated to the synagogue
feet read as thoughts and as shoes
dreams and words weighed together

4.pericope_label: When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it: if thou seest the oppression of the poor, marvel not at the matter

schools.summary: Henry presses the paying rather than the making, gives a Latin tag that whoever is not inclined today will be more averse tomorrow, and finds two reasons against delay, that it affronts God and wrongs ourselves since to vow and not pay incurs treachery where not vowing would have been only an omission; he canvasses three views of the angel without settling, and takes the higher ones for both the angels and the courts of appeal above the princes of provinces.

Gill points out that a vow is an arbitrary thing, not obligatory until made and then binding, and reports one interpreter taking the flesh that is caused to sin as a man’s children, on whom the iniquity may be visited.

Clarke cautions that we are under constant obligation to live to God so that no vow can make it more so, takes the angel for the priest on the authority of a prophet who calls him a messenger of the Lord of hosts while reporting an old paraphrase that makes him the cruel angel of the judgment, turns the verse on dreams into consolation since one who fears God need fear nothing else, and notes that oppression was frequent in provinces far from the seat of power; Wesley also takes the angel for the priest, since the vow made to God was paid to him as one standing in God’s stead.

Ellicott rejects the priestly reading of the angel on three grounds, that the word had not become an ordinary name for the priest, that the priest had no power to dispense with rash vows, and that the phrase is before the angel rather than to the priest, and keeps the sense that a heavenly angel observes and records the vow; he prefers be not dismayed to do not wonder in the last verse and confirms a reading of divine rectification from the author’s habit of verbal assonance; Keil and Delitzsch render the closing clause of one high one watched by another with others above both, and defend an unparalleled phrase against a critic who called it impossible.

debates: Who is the angel before whom the excuse is not to be pleaded? Wesley and Clarke both take it for the priest, Wesley because the vow was paid to him as one standing in God’s stead and Clarke on the authority of a prophet who calls the priest a messenger of the Lord of hosts; Henry canvasses the priest, the guardian angel supposed to attend every man, and the Angel of the covenant, without settling; Ellicott rejects the priest on three separate grounds and keeps a heavenly angel who observes and records the vow.

What does marvel not mean? Ellicott reports the sense of simple surprise, by which the oppression seen is only part of a scheme of mutual wrongdoing in which each oppressor is oppressed by his superior, and prefers be not dismayed, which makes the verse an answer to the gloomy view of the preceding chapter; Henry reads it the second way and takes the higher ones for both angels and human courts of appeal; Clarke takes the marvelling to be at the will of God that permits such evils.
outliers: Ellicott confirms his reading of the closing clause by an argument from style, that the author delights in verbal assonances and constantly links words similar in sound, so that the Hebrew phrase about the high and the higher is meant to suggest the divine name to the reader’s ear.
Ellicott notes the awkwardness of the explanation by which the higher one is the king and those higher still are the women and favourites who govern him.

Clarke turns the verse on dreams into consolation, holding that one who fears God need fear nothing else and that an upright soul may say even to the tempter that because it fears God it does not fear him.
Ellicott reports that the verse on dreams and words presents difficulties of translation springing from corruption of the text, though not such as affect the general sense.
themes: a vow that binds only once made
an angel identified four ways
marvelling turned into dismay
assonance used as evidence
oppressors with oppressors above them

9.pericope_label: The profit of the earth is for all: he that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver

schools.summary: Henry draws a duty of stewardship from the fruits of the earth being for all, adding that dainty meats are only for some, formulates the insatiableness of desire as nature being content with little, grace with less and lust with nothing, observes that ingots of silver satisfy hunger no better than clods of clay and that the more meat the more mouths, and explains the labourer’s sleep by his weariness and digestion and the rich man’s wakefulness by his care, his supper and perhaps his conscience.

Gill offers two senses of the ninth verse beside the usual one, that the excellency of the earth is that God rules above all its oppressors, or that the country is preferable to the city for having fewer tumults, reaches for the horse leech that cries Give, give and observes that a man cannot eat his bags of gold and silver, cites a figure from Xenophon on the growth of a household with its goods, and reports two interpreters of the labouring man, one a tiller of the ground and the other a servant of the Lord.

Clarke reads the ninth verse politically as a joining of head and feet, the peasant protected by the king and the king dependent on the peasant since the wealth of the nation is the fruit of the labourer’s toil, and quotes a Latin line that the love of money increases in proportion as money itself increases.

Keil and Delitzsch take the ninth verse as praise of a patriarchal government founded on agriculture and dispose by name of two rival renderings, one making the king set over the land and the other making him served by its citizens, answering the first from idiom and the second by asking whether a population could be worse designated than by the word for a field; they quote a Latin line that the covetous man is always in want, note that silver is the specific word for coin, distinguish the covetous man from a miser who feeds on looking at his money, and answer the Greek rendering of the labouring man as a slave. Ellicott reports their rendering of the ninth verse as that of many eminent interpreters and calls it hard to clear of the charge of irrelevance, keeping the received English and connecting the verse forward.

debates: How should the ninth verse be rendered? Keil and Delitzsch make it praise of a king devoted to the arable land, and refuse two rival renderings by name, one that sets him over the land and one that has him served by its citizens; Ellicott reports their reading as that of many eminent interpreters and says it is hard to clear of the charge of irrelevance, keeping the received English and connecting the verse with what follows as a consideration meant to mitigate the sight of riches got by oppression; Gill offers two further senses, the rule of God above all oppressors and the preference of country over city.

Who is the labouring man whose sleep is sweet? Keil and Delitzsch report that the Greek renders the word as slave, as if the original had been another word, and answer that sound sleep is the reward of earnest labour, so that since there are idle servants as well as active masters there is no privilege to servants; they prefer the sense of husbandman; Gill reports one interpreter making him a tiller of the ground and another making him a servant of the Lord.
outliers: Henry formulates the insatiableness of desire in one line, that natural desires are at rest when what is desired is obtained but corrupt desires are not, so that nature is content with little, grace with less, and lust with nothing.
Keil and Delitzsch record a Jewish fancy that the word for silver is chosen because its letters rise in value while those of the word for gold decrease.

Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the man of this passage from a miser who shuts his money in chests and feeds himself by looking at it behind closed doors, making him instead a covetous man whose household and disquiet grow with his property.
Henry observes that an empty speculation is all the difference between the owner and those who share with him, since the owner only sees as his own what those about him enjoy the real benefit of.
themes: a king read as servant and as master of the field
money that grows faster than the wish for it
a miser distinguished from a covetous man
sleep broken by supper and by conscience
fruits of the earth held in stewardship

13.pericope_label: Riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt: as he came forth of his mother’s womb, naked shall he return

schools.summary: Henry divides the hurt of riches three ways, the hurt they do their owners, the hurt done with them to others, and the hurt sustained through them since it is the fat beast that is led first to the slaughter, and adds that a very rich man has sometimes been excepted out of a general pardon on account of his estate; he expands the nakedness into swaddling clothes at the entrance and grave clothes at the departure, observes that we are born with our hands griping and die with them extended, and makes the labour for the wind a labour for what has more sound than substance.

Gill takes the eating in darkness generally for a miserable manner of living, coarse bread and sordid apparel and a poor cottage, and reports an interpreter who takes it literally of the night, to which such a man defers eating so as to lose no time from his labour, so that it may not be seen what he eats or how sparingly, and so that others may not eat with him.

Clarke lists four ways in which riches are kept to their owner’s hurt, through improper use, unfortunate partnership, the desire of the robber, or a profligate heir, and says he has seen it again and again; he adopts the variant reading by which the man walks rather than eats in darkness, and quotes a poet on one who counts on long years of pleasure and is quite unfurnished for the world to come; Wesley explains the wrath as the rage of a man cut off before accomplishing his designs and forced to leave the wealth in which all his hopes lie.

Keil and Delitzsch trace the thirteenth and fifteenth verses to the book of Job and report three variants at the seventeenth, two of them supported by the Greek and the Latin and one by a rabbinic commentary and several collated codices, before keeping the received text on the authority of the Targum, an old version and the Masora, and refusing a critic’s construal of the days as object of the verb; Ellicott finds the same use of Job, notes that this passage is in turn used by a later writer, and dismisses the variants of the seventeenth verse in one sentence as not materially affecting the sense.

debates: What is to be done with the variant at the seventeenth verse? Clarke reports that several manuscripts read he walketh for he eateth and adopts it, so that the man walks in darkness with no evidence of salvation; Keil and Delitzsch report that variant and two others, note which versions support each, and keep the received text on the authority of the Targum, an old version and the Masora; Ellicott, elsewhere the readiest of them to emend, passes the whole question by in one sentence as not materially affecting the sense.
outliers: Clarke lists four ways in which riches are kept to their owner’s hurt, through improper use that costs him his health, an unfortunate partnership, the desire of the robber who may take his life as well as his goods, or a profligate heir, and adds that he has seen this again and again.
Henry observes that a very rich man has sometimes been excepted out of a general pardon, in life and estate alike, merely on account of his vast and overgrown estate.

Henry sets the swaddling clothes friends provide at a man’s entrance against the grave clothes they provide at his departure, and adds that we are born with our hands griping but die with them extended, letting go what we held fast.

Gill reports an interpreter who takes the eating in darkness literally of the night, to which the covetous man defers his meal so as to lose no working time, so that his poor fare may not be seen, and so that no one may eat with him.
themes: four ways for wealth to ruin its owner
a variant adopted, weighed and ignored
hands griping at birth and open at death
a supper postponed to hide its poverty
anger at providence doubling an affliction

18.pericope_label: It is good and comely to eat and to drink and to enjoy the good of all his labour: for it is his portion

schools.summary: Henry infers from the vanity of hoarded riches that the sober use of what Providence allots is both duty and decency, fixes the limits on both sides against indulgence of the flesh and against starving oneself through covetousness or through excessive care and grief, and takes the promise of the last verse to mean that a cheerful spirit makes the yoke of our employments easy and the burden of our afflictions light.

Gill reads the closing verse two ways, first in the received sense that the contented man will not think life long and tedious nor distress himself with the troubles he has met, then in the sense given by an interpreter he approves and which he says agrees with the accents, that if he has not much he remembers how few his days are and is content, calling to mind how he has been supplied hitherto.

Clarke holds that God gives every man the necessaries of life in the course of his providence and wills that he thankfully use them, so that earthly blessings are as truly the portion of the body as the salvation of God is the portion of the soul, and Wesley draws the same line by glossing the portion as one of worldly goods with a better portion in heaven.

Keil and Delitzsch note that the opening word marks a return to a conclusion already reached, that the following verse is constructed without proper sequence and cannot be so rendered into English, and that the enjoyment is not made possible by the possession of earthly treasures but is a special gift added thereto; Ellicott records only that the Preacher is led back to his earlier conclusion.

debates: How is the closing verse to be taken? Gill reports and approves an accentuation that reverses it, so that the man who has little remembers how few his days are and is content, rather than the man who has enough forgetting his troubles. Keil and Delitzsch keep the received sense, that over this enjoyment he forgets the frailty and the darkened side of life, marking one explanation of it incorrect and endorsing a second in its revised form; and they note that an ancient version read the verb as occupies rather than answers, which would have required a different form of the word, while Jerome helped that reading by taking a different noun with it. Ellicott states the usual explanation, says he is not satisfied with it, and adds that he cannot suggest a better.
outliers: Ellicott states the common explanation of the last verse, declares himself unsatisfied with it, and offers no alternative, the only voice here to record dissatisfaction without proposing a remedy.
Henry warns against the opposite error to covetousness in the same breath, that a man may starve himself through excessive care and grief as well as through greed.
Gill answers the verse with an inventory rather than an exposition, counting estate personal and real and goods movable and immovable as the substance in view.
Keil and Delitzsch rest the whole weight of the verse on a grammatical irregularity they say cannot be carried over into English at all.
themes: a conclusion returned to, not advanced
good to oneself and comely to others
the portion of the body and the portion of the soul
an accentuation that reverses the sense
troubles remembered as waters that pass away
